ABSTRACT: Chiral allenyl phosphine oxides hold significant
application value in organic synthesis, serving as efficient catalysts,
ligands, and versatile synthons. However, the development of
transition metal-catalyzed asymmetric synthesis for these com-
pounds remains unexplored, primarily due to the facile tautome-
rization of phosphine oxides into trivalent R
1
R
2
P−OH species,
which may severely deactivate transition metal catalysts through
strong coordination interactions. Herein, a ligand relay strategy has
been applied to address this challenge in the Pd-catalyzed
enantioselective coupling reactions of propargylic benzoates and secondary phosphine oxides (SPOs) to afford chiral trisubstituted
allenyl phosphine oxides with high ee. The ligand relay protocol involves the initial coordination of a palladium catalyst with readily
available triphenylphosphine, followed by dynamic ligand exchange with the stretchable chiral ligand DACH-ZYC-Phos-C1 (L26),
while PPh
3
does not work as a nonchiral ligand for palladium catalysts in this transformation. Chiral trivalent organophosphines with
high ee have been obtained upon the reduction of allenyl phosphine oxides. Mechanistic studies revealed the nature of the kinetic
resolution. DFT calculations provide a mechanistic rationale for the observed high enantioselectivity and superior catalytic efficiency,
which is governed by the ligand L26 through steric repulsions that selectively destabilize the disfavored oxidative addition transition
states.
■
INTRODUCTION
The introduction of a phosphine oxide group into molecules
usually results in a dramatic change in their physical and
chemical properties, which has attracted more and more
attention. As a versatile functional unit, phosphine oxide
groups have been widely applied in functional materials,
1
medicine,
2
catalysts,
3
and ligands for metal catalysts.
4
Of
particular interest, phosphine oxides with an allene function-
ality are not only useful catalysts (Scheme 1a)
5
but also
important synthons.
6−9
Recently, much attention has been
paid to the synthesis and chemistry of allenes.
10−13
However, a
transition metal-catalyzed asymmetric approach for allenyl
phosphine oxides has not been developed due to the facile
tautomerization of phosphine oxide into the trivalent R
1
R
2
P−
OH, which may severely poison the transition metal via
extensive coordination (Scheme 1b).
14
Specifically, the energy
barrier for the isomerization of secondary phosphine oxides
(SPOs) to trivalent R
1
R
2
P−OH is much lower than that of H-
phosphonates.
15
Thus, the rate constant of SPO-to-R
1
R
2
P−
OH is significantly higher than that of H-phosphonates
(Scheme 1b), which reduces both the rate of formation and
the catalytic activity of the envisioned chiral transition metal
catalyst with the M-L* unit (Scheme 1c). Furthermore, such
nonchiral metal-R
1
R
2
P−OH coordination may also promote
nonchiral background reactions, thereby reducing enantiose-
lectivity, which further makes the synthesis of chiral allenyl
phosphine oxides more challenging.
16
To address this issue, we
propose that a ligand relay strategy may provide a solution,
whereby the transition metal catalyst first coordinates with an
achiral ligand L, followed by ligand exchange with a chiral
ligand L*, to form the corresponding catalytically active species
M-L* (Scheme 1c). To realize this proposed strategy, the
exploration of readily available ligand L and a flexible chiral
ligand L* emerges as a key strategy. Herein, we report such a
ligand relay strategy for chiral palladium catalysis, enabling the
catalytic enantioselective synthesis of chiral trisubstituted
allenyl phosphine oxides through the coupling reactions of
propargylic benzoates with SPOs. This is achieved via the
synergistic cooperation of DACH-ZYC-Phos-C1 as the chiral
entity and triphenylphosphine (PPh
3
) as the relay ligand
(Scheme 1d).

configuration in the allenyl products based on a previous
report.

The subsequent anti-oxidative addition of (S)-INT1 proceeds
via (S)-TS1, which requires an activation energy of 14.2 kcal/
mol, resulting in the formation of the π-propargyl-Pd
intermediate (S)-INT2. Further coordination of diphenylphos-
phine oxide 2a to the Pd(II) center leads to the generation of
either the η-1 coordinated allenyl palladium intermediate (S)-
INT3 or the propargyl palladium intermediate (S)-INT3′. The
latter, (S)- INT3′, is thermodynamically less stable than (S)-
INT3 by 5.5 kcal/mol and thus energetically unfavorable.
Deprotonation of (S)-INT3 by the OBz
−
anion then proceeds
through (S)-TS2, with an activation barrier of 15.3 kcal/mol,
yielding (S)-INT4 and simultaneously facilitating the trans-
formation of pentavalent to trivalent phosphine. Subsequently,
ligand exchange between phosphine and oxygen on the
palladium center in (S)-INT4 proceeds via (S)-TS3, requiring
a free energy of 16.7 kcal/mol. This step produces the
phosphoryl palladium intermediate (S)-INT5, which is
exergonic by 8.1 kcal/mol (relative to (S)-INT1). Finally,
the reductive elimination of (S)-INT5 occurs with an energy
barrier of 12.3 kcal/mol ((S)-TS4), generating the R-
configured major product, allenyl phosphine oxide (R)-3aa,
while simultaneously introducing another molecule of (S)-1a
to regenerate (S)-INT1, thereby completing the catalytic cycle.
Consequently, the Pd−P bond formation step via (S)-TS3 is
identified as both the rate-limiting and enantiodetermining
step, with the highest free energy barrier of 16.7 kcal/mol
throughout the whole process. In contrast, the free energy
profile corresponding to the minor enantiomer of (S)-3aa
(gray line in Figure 1a), yielded from the mismatched
combination of (S)-1a with (R,R)-L26, exhibits a similar
pathway but with higher energy demands, particularly in the
oxidative addition step ((R)-TS1, 19.3 kcal/mol). This
indicates that oxidative addition is both the rate-limiting and
enantioselectivity-determining step for the (S)-3aa formation.
The calculated enantioselectivity, based on the free energy
difference of 2.6 kcal/mol between (R)-TS1 and (S)-TS3,
predicts a 98% enantiomeric excess (ee) favoring the R
enantiomer, which aligns well with the experimental ee value of
91%.

2.21 Å) in (R)-TS1 destabilize the transition state. In the
absence of the steric hindrance, (S)-TS1 is more favorable than
(R)-TS1 by 6.4 kcal/mol in overall electronic energy,
highlighting the critical role of the steric effect of the ligand
with the substrate in governing the enantioselectivity of the
reaction.
According to these results, a possible reaction pathway was
proposed, as shown in Scheme 6. The Pd(0) catalyst first
coordinated with PPh
3
followed by ligand exchange with the
chiral ligand L26 to form the active catalyst Pd-L26, which
would undergo a much faster anti-oxidative addition

(S)-1 to give the allenyl Pd(II) intermediate (R)-Int-I.
Subsequent ligand exchange between (R)-Int-I and SPO
would form (R)-Int-II while releasing one molecule of benzoic
acid. After reductive elimination, the desired product (R)-3
was produced along with the chiral Pd(0) catalyst.

CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we have successfully developed a relay ligand
effect between PPh
3
and DACH-ZYC-Phos, enabling an
efficient Pd-catalyzed asymmetric coupling of propargylic
benzoates and secondary phosphine oxides (SPOs) for the
synthesis of chiral allenyl phosphine oxides with excellent
enantioselectivity. The corresponding products could be
further converted into various phosphorus compounds without
racemization. Importantly, the chiral allenyl phosphine oxide
could be reduced to the chiral allenyl phosphine, which may
have potential applications in asymmetric catalysis. Preliminary
mechanistic studies indicated the kinetic resolution nature of
this process. The observed enantioselectivity has been
rationalized by DFT studies. Further studies on the mechanism
and related reactions are currently ongoing in our laboratory.
